quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the /d/ at the end of "hard". With another consonant right before it and another right after (from "time"), can a speaker realistically hit all three cleanly?
quests.explanation: This is elision: a sound is removed entirely, not changed or weakened. Here, the /d/ at the end of "hard" disappears before the consonant that starts "time".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try saying "intend fully" at a natural conversational pace, not word by word. What happens to the /d/ sound in the middle?
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce every consonant in a heavy cluster. In "intend fully", the /d/ is left out completely, letting the surrounding consonants connect directly.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Three consonants in a row is hard work for the mouth. Focus on the /t/ where "first" meets "prize" — does English keep it or drop it?
quests.explanation: Because /t/ is squeezed between two other consonants, it gets dropped in fluent speech. Say "first prize" aloud and you'll notice the /t/ just isn't there.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "miss" ends in /s/ and "you" begins with a /j/ sound. What single new consonant do the two combine into?
quests.explanation: When /s/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two often fuse into a single new consonant. In "miss you", /s/ + /j/ becomes /ʃ/ — a completely different sound from either original.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The tongue is already anticipating "copy"'s velar sound before it even finishes "hard". What happens to /d/ as a result?
quests.explanation: The change from /d/ to /g/ at the end of "hard" happens because the following velar consonant in "copy" pulls the place of articulation to match. Nothing is lost here, just reshaped.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Between "good" and "morning" sits a consonant under pressure to match its neighbor. What does it become?
quests.explanation: This pairing is a classic assimilation example: the /d/ ending "good" adopts the bilabial quality of the sound in "morning", surfacing as /b/ in natural, connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In casual speech, does the final /t/ of "rent" get pronounced before "free", or does it just vanish?
quests.explanation: English speakers simplify clusters like this one by deleting a stop consonant rather than forcing it in. The /t/ in "rent" is the one that goes missing before "free".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This isn't a case of a sound vanishing from "seven" — it's still there, just different. What does /n/ turn into before the velar sound in "cans"?
quests.explanation: Notice that the /n/ ending "seven" isn't deleted the way it would be in elision — it survives, just transformed into /ŋ/ to match the velar sound beginning "cans".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Picture how a native speaker would say "best wishes" in a fast, everyday sentence. Is every single consonant still there?
quests.explanation: This is a textbook case of consonant-cluster elision: the /t/ between two consonants is dropped to keep speech fluent and effortless in "best wishes".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Instead of hearing /s/ and /j/ separately between "this" and "year", listen for one fused sound. What is it?
quests.explanation: This is coalescent assimilation: two adjacent sounds merge into a third sound that resembles neither one alone. Here, /s/ and /j/ combine into /ʃ/ in "this year".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "background" is trapped between two other consonants right before "check". What usually happens to a stop consonant stuck in that position?
quests.explanation: Rather than pronounce all three consonants back to back, speakers cut the /d/ from "background" entirely. The result flows straight from the first consonant into "check".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen closely at the boundary of "last" and "night" — count the consonants stacking up. Does the /t/ still make it into the sentence?
quests.explanation: In fast, connected speech, a /t/ wedged between consonants almost always disappears. That's what you'll hear in "last night" — the /t/ goes silent.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "expect more" naturally, without pausing between the words. Is the /t/ audible, or does it disappear into the next consonant?
quests.explanation: Elision removes a sound completely rather than merely blending it. Here the /t/ vanishes from "expect" so the phrase moves directly into "more".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ at the end of "get" is about to meet a bilabial sound in "paid". Does it hold firm, or shift to match?
quests.explanation: Before a bilabial consonant, /t/ commonly shifts to match its place of articulation. In "get paid", /t/ becomes /p/ — the sound itself changes, it doesn't disappear.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This pair, "paint dries", creates a tricky consonant sequence. Which sound do fluent speakers simplify away — and is it really gone, or just quieter?
quests.explanation: Speakers naturally avoid three consonants in a row, so the /t/ is dropped rather than forced through. That's why "paint dries" sounds smoother without it.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "not clear" at natural speed. Listen right at the boundary — does the /t/ stay a /t/, or does it become something else?
quests.explanation: This is regressive assimilation: a sound changes to become more like the sound that follows it. Here, the /t/ ending "not" turns into /k/ because "clear" begins with a velar consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A velar consonant is coming up in "coat". What does that do to the /n/ just before it in "brown"?
quests.explanation: Speakers save effort by letting /n/ anticipate the velar sound ahead. So in "brown coat", /n/ is pronounced as /ŋ/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "read your" quickly and casually. The /d/ and the /j/ in "your" don't stay separate — what do they merge into?
quests.explanation: Rather than two separate consonants, connected speech blends /d/ and /j/ into /dʒ/. That's why "read your" sounds like one smooth unit rather than two words bumping together.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Fluent speech avoids awkward consonant pile-ups. Where exactly does that simplification happen in "hand baggage"?
quests.explanation: This cluster is simplified by deleting the /d/ altogether — not weakening it, not shifting it, just leaving it out — which is the defining feature of elision in "hand baggage".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant collision at the boundary of "meet" and "you": /t/ meets /j/. Which single sound comes out the other side?
quests.explanation: Coalescence happens when neighboring sounds are so close in the mouth that they collapse into one. /t/ and /j/ become /tʃ/ in "meet you" — faster and easier to say than keeping the two sounds apart.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "talked" alone, then "back" alone — both consonants are clear. Now blend them at speed. What happens to the /t/ in between?
quests.explanation: Notice that nothing replaces the /t/ — it isn't weakened or swapped for another sound, it's simply omitted. That full deletion is what separates elision from assimilation in "talked back".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A stop consonant squeezed between two other consonants rarely survives in fast speech. Listen for the /d/ in "behind schedule" — is it there?
quests.explanation: Consonant clusters like this one are common at word boundaries in English, and the middle stop is almost always the casualty. The /d/ drops out of "behind schedule" for exactly that reason.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two consonants become one here. Focus on where "place" ends and "your" begins — what's the resulting blended sound?
quests.explanation: This merge is extremely common wherever a word ending in /s/ meets a "you"-type word. In "place your", the result is /ʃ/, not /s/ followed by /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Rather than pronouncing /s/ then /j/ separately, fluent speakers coalesce them. What do you actually hear in "promise yourself"?
quests.explanation: Notice that neither the original /s/ nor /j/ survives on its own — they combine into /ʃ/. That fusion is what makes "promise yourself" sound natural and fast.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /n/ ending "seven" to the bilabial sound that opens "points". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /n/ becomes /m/ in "seven points" to match the bilabial consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen at natural speed: does "should you" keep two distinct consonant sounds at the boundary, or blend them into a new one?
quests.explanation: In relaxed, natural speech, /d/ and /j/ rarely stay separate at a word boundary like this one. They coalesce into /dʒ/, exactly as in "should you".
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ in "didn't" and the /j/ starting "you" don't survive as separate sounds in fast speech. What do they turn into together?
quests.explanation: This is why "didn't you" doesn't sound like two crisp, separate words: the boundary consonant /t/ and the /j/ of "you" merge into the single sound /tʃ/.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a sound-merging boundary. What new consonant replaces /t/ + /j/ when you say "can't you" naturally?
quests.explanation: Coalescence is a genuine sound change, not just fast talking — /t/ plus /j/ reliably becomes /tʃ/ in phrases like "can't you" across natural English speech.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "ten" to "girls". Is it still /n/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in /n/ meets a velar sound, the /n/ shifts to /ŋ/ so both sounds are made in nearly the same place in the mouth. That's what happens in "ten girls".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try blending "had" straight into "your" without a pause. The /d/ and /j/ fuse — into what sound?
quests.explanation: The two sounds don't just sit next to each other; they blend into /dʒ/. That's the defining feature of coalescence, and it's exactly what happens in "had your".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".
